views.name: film_with_language_category
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  f.film_id,
  f.title,
  f.description,
  f.release_year,
  f.language_id,
  l.name AS name,
  f.original_language_id,
  f.rental_duration,
  f.rental_rate,
  f.length,
  f.replacement_cost,
  f.rating,
  f.special_features,
  fc.category_id,
  c.name AS category_name,
  f.last_update
FROM film f
LEFT JOIN language l ON f.language_id = l.language_id
LEFT JOIN film_category fc ON f.film_id = fc.film_id
LEFT JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id

params.description: Provides film-level rows expanded with their language and category membership — one row per (film_id, category_id).
params.when_to_use: Listing films together with their assigned category and display language. | Joining film attributes (title, release year, rates, length, rating) to category-level analyses (e.g., counts by category) where film-category is the desired grain. | Building catalogs, UI lists, or reports that need both film metadata and the category name.
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating at the film-only grain (film_id) without handling multiple categories: this view is at film-category grain, so aggregating per film without DISTINCT or re-aggregation will double-count films that belong to multiple categories. | Using it as if it were a single-row-per-film dimension when joining to transactions (rentals/payments): because film_id may appear multiple times (one per category), joining directly will multiply measures from one-to-many downstream facts. | Expecting language or category to always exist: LEFT JOINs mean language or category fields can be NULL; assuming non-NULL will cause logic errors. | Attempting to compute aggregates that require deduplication (e.g., count of unique films): using COUNT(*) on this view yields counts at film-category grain, not distinct film counts.
params.output_schema: film_id: unique identifier of the film (source: film.film_id) | title: film title (source: film.title) | description: film description/summary (source: film.description) | release_year: year the film was released (source: film.release_year) | language_id: language identifier for the film (source: film.language_id) | name: name of the language mapped from language.language_id (source: language.name aliased as name) | original_language_id: original language id for the film, if any (source: film.original_language_id) | rental_duration: allowed rental duration for the film (source: film.rental_duration) | rental_rate: rental price for the film (source: film.rental_rate) | length: running time / length of the film (source: film.length) | replacement_cost: cost to replace the film (source: film.replacement_cost) | rating: film rating (e.g., G, PG) (source: film.rating) | special_features: film special features metadata (source: film.special_features) | category_id: identifier of the category assigned to the film (source: film_category.category_id) | category_name: human-readable category name (source: category.name aliased as category_name) | last_update: last update timestamp for the film record (source: film.last_update)
params.grounded_columns: film.film_id | film.title | film.description | film.release_year | film.language_id | language.name | film.original_language_id | film.rental_duration | film.rental_rate | film.length | film.replacement_cost | film.rating | film.special_features | film_category.category_id | category.name | film.last_update
params.metric: No aggregated metrics are defined in this view. All columns are passed-through base columns or direct lookups. Derived measures must be computed by downstream queries with attention to the view's film_id x category_id grain.
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: Join to a single-row-per-film table or view on film_id (e.g., a film dimension that is strictly one row per film) — safe because this view already contains one or more rows per film but joining to a single-row-per-film will not multiply rows. | Cardinality-SAFE: Join to the language table/view on language_id (or to language dimension) — language is one-to-many only from language to film, and here the join was a LEFT JOIN from film to language; joining additional language attributes is safe because language rows are one-per-language_id. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables such as inventory, rentals, payments, or any view that is at a finer grain (e.g., inventory_with_film_store, rentals_by_inventory_agg if it is at inventory/rental grain) without aggregation/deduplication — joining them will multiply this view's film-category rows and thereby duplicate measures (e.g., counts, sums) unless you pre-aggregate the fact side to the film_id (or film_id,category_id) grain. | If you need film-level (distinct film) metrics, first aggregate this view by film_id (e.g., SELECT film_id, MIN(title) ... and COUNT(DISTINCT film_id) semantics) or join to a true one-row-per-film dimension to avoid multi-category duplication. | When joining to category-level aggregates, join on category_id and ensure the aggregate is one-row-per-category so you don't change the film-category cardinality unexpectedly.
params.comparison: Use inventory_with_film_store instead when you need film rows augmented with inventory and store-level location details — inventory_with_film_store provides inventory/store context and is at a finer grain (inventory) whereas this view is film x category grain. | Use film_length_and_rate_norm when you need normalized length and rate metrics (e.g., z-scores or scaled values) — that sibling likely contains derived normalized measures; this view provides raw length and rental_rate only. | Do not substitute this view for payments_by_customer_agg, rentals_by_inventory_agg, or other aggregate views when you require pre-aggregated metrics — those siblings are aggregated and safe to join to at their aggregate grain, while this view is a join (non-aggregated) at film-category grain. | Use latest_rental_per_inventory_rank or top_actors_by_film_count_rank when you need ranking/windowed results — those siblings provide rank/windowed outputs while this view exposes base film/category attributes.

views.description: Denormalized film-level relation enriched with language and category names. One row per film-category (preserves film-category multiplicity). Useful as a starting point for catalog queries, counts by category/language, and joins to inventory/rental. | Use for: List films and their categories or languages; Aggregate film counts or average rental_rate by category or language; Filter films by category_name or language name

views.name: inventory_with_film_store
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  i.inventory_id,
  i.film_id,
  f.title AS title,
  i.store_id,
  s.address_id AS address_id,
  a.city_id AS city_id,
  ci.country_id AS country_id,
  ci.city AS city,
  co.country AS country,
  i.last_update
FROM inventory i
LEFT JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
LEFT JOIN store s ON i.store_id = s.store_id
LEFT JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
LEFT JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
LEFT JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id

params.description: Provides one-row-per-inventory item enriched with its film title and the store's hierarchical location (address → city → country) and last update timestamp.
params.when_to_use: Look up metadata for a specific inventory_id (film, store, address, city, country, last_update). | Build a catalog or inventory listing showing which film copy (inventory) is in which store and its location details. | Join inventory-level data to other datasets where the inventory_id grain is required (e.g., attach film/store/location attributes to inventory-level facts).
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating counts, sums, or other measures at film, store, city, or country level without re-aggregation — the view is at inventory_id grain, so summing here then joining to other tables risks double counting if not careful. | Forming cohorts or time-window aggregates (e.g., rentals per inventory over time) — this view carries no rental/payment/time aggregation and using it as if it were temporal aggregate will yield incorrect results. | Joining to one-to-many child tables (rentals, payments) without first aggregating them to inventory_id — doing so will multiply inventory rows and produce inflated measures (mis-count). | Using it as a film-level canonical source — multiple inventory rows map to the same film_id; treating this view as one-row-per-film will silently duplicate film-level metrics.
params.output_schema: inventory_id: Unique identifier for an inventory item. Derived from inventory.inventory_id. | film_id: Identifier of the film assigned to this inventory item. Derived from inventory.film_id. | title: Film title for the film_id on this inventory row. Derived from film.title (joined via film.film_id = inventory.film_id). | store_id: Identifier of the store that holds this inventory item. Derived from inventory.store_id. | address_id: Identifier of the store's address. Derived from store.address_id (joined via store.store_id = inventory.store_id). | city_id: Identifier of the city for the store's address. Derived from address.city_id (joined via address.address_id = store.address_id). | country_id: Identifier of the country for the store's city. Derived from city.country_id (joined via city.city_id = address.city_id). | city: City name for the store's address. Derived from city.city (joined via city.city_id = address.city_id). | country: Country name for the store's city. Derived from country.country (joined via country.country_id = city.country_id). | last_update: Timestamp showing last update of the inventory row. Derived from inventory.last_update.
params.grounded_columns: inventory.inventory_id | inventory.film_id | inventory.store_id | inventory.last_update | film.film_id | film.title | store.store_id | store.address_id | address.address_id | address.city_id | city.city_id | city.country_id | city.city | country.country_id | country.country
params.metric: No aggregate metrics are defined in this view; all output columns are base attributes projected from underlying tables (no SUM/COUNT/AVG/etc).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE: You may JOIN this view to dimension-like, one-row-per-key views/tables on inventory_id or store_id (for example, join to latest_rental_per_inventory_rank on inventory_id if that ranking view is one-row-per-inventory) because those joins are 1:1 and will not duplicate rows. | cardinality-SAFE: JOIN to film_with_language_category on film_id is safe if that sibling view is strictly one-row-per-film (confirm film_with_language_category's grain); joining on film_id will map each inventory row to film attributes without duplicating inventory-level measures. | DO NOT JOIN to rentals, payments, rentals_by_inventory_agg, or other one-to-many children directly without aggregation: joining inventory_with_film_store (one-row-per-inventory) to a raw rentals table (many rentals per inventory) will multiply inventory rows and cause inflated counts/sums. Instead, aggregate rentals/payments to inventory_id first (for example via rentals_by_inventory_agg) and then join 1:1. | DO NOT JOIN to sibling aggregates (payments_by_customer_agg, rentals_by_inventory_agg) on higher-grain keys (e.g., customer_id, film_id) without re-aggregating or changing grain — mismatched grains cause cohort/aggregation anti-patterns. | If you need film-level aggregates, first aggregate inventory rows to film_id (e.g., count(inventory_id) grouped by film_id) and then join to film-level views; directly aggregating after joining film attributes here can still be valid but be explicit about GROUP BY film_id to avoid accidental row-multiplication.
params.comparison: use film_with_language_category instead when you need film-level attributes (language, category) and expect one-row-per-film — that view is designed for film grain, whereas inventory_with_film_store is one-row-per-inventory and will have multiple rows per film. | use rentals_by_inventory_agg when you need rental aggregations at the inventory grain (counts, last rental timestamp) — rentals_by_inventory_agg provides pre-aggregated measures safe to join 1:1 to this view on inventory_id. | use payments_by_customer_agg or customer_payment_rfm when analyzing customer payment behavior — those are customer-grain aggregates and are not interchangeable with this inventory-grain view. | use latest_rental_per_inventory_rank when you need exactly one latest rental row per inventory (ranked) — it complements this view by providing rental facts at the inventory grain suitable for 1:1 joins.

views.description: Inventory items joined to film and store/location info (via address -> city -> country). One row per inventory item. Useful for stock-levels, store-level availability, and joining to rental/payment events. | Use for: Which stores have which inventory items; Counts of inventory by store/city/country; Join inventory to rental/payment events for turnover analysis

views.name: customer_with_location
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.store_id,
  c.first_name,
  c.last_name,
  c.email,
  c.address_id,
  a.address AS address,
  a.address2 AS address2,
  a.district AS district,
  a.postal_code AS postal_code,
  a.phone AS phone,
  a.city_id AS city_id,
  ci.city AS city,
  ci.country_id AS country_id,
  co.country AS country,
  c.active,
  c.create_date,
  c.last_update
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
LEFT JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
LEFT JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id

params.description: A one-row-per-customer enriched with that customer's postal and geographic location (address, city, country) and basic contact/metadata.
params.when_to_use: Looking up customer contact info and location for a single customer or a set of customers (email, phone, address, city, country). | Joining customer-level attributes (active flag, create_date, last_update) to other customer-keyed datasets. | Reporting or exporting customer address directories where each row should represent one customer.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to transactional tables (payments, rentals, inventory, etc.) to compute aggregates without re-aggregation — doing so can silently duplicate customer rows and over-count metrics because transactional tables are one-to-many to customers. | Using this to compute cohort or time-windowed metrics that require per-event rows (e.g., count of rentals per customer over time). This view is grain = customer_id, so event-level time-series must come from rental/payment sources. | Joining to a table/view that is one-to-many to customer (for example payments_by_customer_agg if expanded back to payments) without first aggregating the many-side to customer_id — otherwise counts, sums and rates will be multiplied. | Assuming address, city, or country are always present (this view uses LEFT JOINs). Missing address/city/country will result in NULLs — queries that require non-null locations should filter accordingly.
params.output_schema: customer_id: the customer identifier — derives from customer.customer_id | store_id: store that the customer is associated with — derives from customer.store_id | first_name: customer's first name — derives from customer.first_name | last_name: customer's last name — derives from customer.last_name | email: customer's email address — derives from customer.email | address_id: FK to address table on customer.address_id — derives from customer.address_id | address: primary street address text — derives from address.address | address2: secondary street address text — derives from address.address2 | district: district/region for the address — derives from address.district | postal_code: postal code for the address — derives from address.postal_code | phone: phone number from the address record — derives from address.phone | city_id: FK to city table as stored on address.city_id — derives from address.city_id | city: city name — derives from city.city | country_id: FK to country as stored on city.country_id — derives from city.country_id | country: country name — derives from country.country | active: boolean/int flag whether customer is active — derives from customer.active | create_date: when the customer record was created — derives from customer.create_date | last_update: last update timestamp for the customer record — derives from customer.last_update
params.grounded_columns: customer.customer_id | customer.store_id | customer.first_name | customer.last_name | customer.email | customer.address_id | address.address_id | address.address | address.address2 | address.district | address.postal_code | address.phone | address.city_id | city.city_id | city.city | city.country_id | country.country_id | country.country | customer.active | customer.create_date | customer.last_update
params.metric: No aggregated metrics are produced by this view. All columns are base attributes propagated from the underlying tables. (Expressed another way: there are no derived aggregates: derived_col = <none>.)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customer-keyed dimensions or one-row-per-customer views on customer_id — safe because this view's grain is one row per customer_id and such joins will not duplicate rows. | Safe: join to a view that is also one-row-per-customer (for example a customer_preference view keyed by customer_id) ON customer_id — preserves one-row-per-customer. | Safe: join to store-level or country-level dimension tables on store_id or country_id — these are many-to-one toward this view (store or country keyed), so they will not multiply rows. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables (payments, rentals, inventory, etc.) without pre-aggregating those tables to customer_id first. Example anti-pattern: customer_with_location JOIN rentals r ON customer_id will multiply customer rows by each rental, causing mis-counts if you then sum rental amounts. | If you need customer-level aggregates from payments or rentals, either use the pre-aggregated sibling aggregate views (payments_by_customer_agg, rentals_by_inventory_agg aggregated appropriately) or aggregate payments/rentals to customer_id before joining to this view. This ensures cardinality is preserved and metrics are correct.
params.comparison: use payments_by_customer_agg instead when you need summed payment metrics per customer — payments_by_customer_agg provides aggregated financial measures; customer_with_location provides only contact/location attributes and will not supply correct payment totals. | use rentals_by_inventory_agg when you need inventory- or rental-event level aggregations — customer_with_location is at customer grain and lacks event-level rows. | use staff_activity_join when you need staff-centric activity mixes — staff_activity_join targets staff/activity grain whereas this view is customer-centric. | use customer_payment_rfm when you need RFM (recency/frequency/monetary) scoring per customer — that sibling performs windowed/aggregated computations; customer_with_location only supplies demographic/location attributes. | use other JOIN-type sibling views (film_with_language_category, inventory_with_film_store) when you need film or inventory centric enrichment — those siblings have a different grain (film or inventory) and are inappropriate for customer-centric queries.

views.description: Customer rows enriched with address, city and country for geographic analysis. One row per customer. Useful for customer segmentation, regional reporting, and joins to payments/rentals. | Use for: Customer lists by city or country; Active vs inactive customer counts by region; Joining customers to payments and rentals for regional revenue

views.name: payments_by_customer_agg
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.customer_id,
  COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payment_count,
  SUM(p.amount) AS total_payment_amount,
  MIN(p.payment_date) AS first_payment_date,
  MAX(p.payment_date) AS last_payment_date
FROM payment p
GROUP BY p.customer_id

params.description: Per-customer payment aggregates: count, sum, first and last payment dates for each customer_id.
params.when_to_use: Answering questions about total payments or number of payments per customer (e.g., lifetime spend, number of transactions). | Joining a customer-level payment metric into customer profiles or reports where one row per customer is desired. | Feeding customer-level features into models (RFM, churn, CLV) that expect aggregated payment metrics at the customer granularity.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to a table that has multiple rows per customer (e.g., payment, rental, inventory) expecting per-payment detail — doing so and then aggregating again without careful handling will double-count or multiply measures because this view is already aggregated to customer level. | Using this view to answer time-windowed cohort queries (e.g., payments in last 30 days) without restricting or re-aggregating the underlying payment table — the view is lifetime (no date filter) and will return full-history aggregates, so it silently gives wrong cohorts. | Treating payment_count as distinct transaction count when joins or filters elsewhere introduce duplicates — if you join this AGG to a table that duplicates customers, counting rows of the joined result (instead of using the payment_count column) will mis-count. | Expecting first_payment_date or last_payment_date to reflect any partition/window (e.g., first payment within a campaign) — these are MIN/MAX over all payments in the payment table for a customer.
params.output_schema: customer_id: Surrogate/PK of the customer; sourced from payment.customer_id (grouping key). | payment_count: Number of payments for the customer; derived from COUNT(payment.payment_id) over all rows in payment per customer. | total_payment_amount: Sum of amounts paid by the customer; derived from SUM(payment.amount) over all payment rows per customer. | first_payment_date: Earliest payment_date observed for the customer; derived from MIN(payment.payment_date) per customer. | last_payment_date: Latest payment_date observed for the customer; derived from MAX(payment.payment_date) per customer.
params.metric: payment_count = COUNT(payment.payment_id) -- cardinality of payments per customer | total_payment_amount = SUM(payment.amount) -- total monetary amount across payments per customer | first_payment_date = MIN(payment.payment_date) -- earliest payment_date for the customer | last_payment_date = MAX(payment.payment_date) -- latest payment_date for the customer
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to customer_with_location ON customer_id — safe because this view is one-row-per-customer, so joining to the one-row-per-customer view will not duplicate payment measures. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to film_with_language_category, inventory_with_film_store, staff_activity_join only when those joins are performed via a customer-level key that is one-to-one; in practice these siblings are not customer-level and require care. | Do NOT join this AGG directly to payment (the base table) expecting to preserve counts — joining back to payment will create one row per payment and will duplicate this AGG data unless you drop AGG measures or re-aggregate from payment. | Do NOT join this AGG to rentals_by_inventory_agg or latest_rental_per_inventory_rank without re-aggregating: those views are inventory- or rental-grain and can have many rows per customer when related via rentals/inventory, which would multiply payment_count and total_payment_amount unless you aggregate after the join. | If you need customer-level metrics combined with many-to-one or many-to-many dimensions (for example customers × stores or customers × films), either: (a) join this AGG to the one-row-per-customer dimension only, or (b) join dimensions first and then re-aggregate payment measures from the payment table directly to the desired composite grain (recommended).
params.comparison: Use customer_with_location instead when you need customer attributes (address, city, etc.) joined at customer granularity — it's a JOIN sibling that provides dimensional attributes while this AGG provides payment metrics. | Use rentals_by_inventory_agg when your analysis is inventory- or rental-centric (e.g., number of rentals per inventory) — rentals_by_inventory_agg is aggregated at inventory/rental grain and will not provide correct per-customer payment aggregates. | Use customer_payment_rfm when you need RFM-style recency/frequency/monetary features computed with windows/partitions — customer_payment_rfm may apply different window logic or filtering (e.g., recency relative to a reference date), whereas payments_by_customer_agg is a simple lifetime aggregation.

views.description: Aggregated payment measures per customer: total amount, payment_count, first and last payment dates. One row per customer. Useful for lifetime value, recency/frequency/monetary (RFM) analyses. | Use for: Customer lifetime value and revenue per customer; RFM segmentation using recency, frequency, monetary measures; Identify customers with no payments (LEFT JOIN against customer)

views.name: rentals_by_inventory_agg
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  r.inventory_id,
  COUNT(r.rental_id) AS rental_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.return_date IS NOT NULL AND r.rental_date IS NOT NULL THEN
    (julianday(r.return_date) - julianday(r.rental_date))
    ELSE 0 END) AS total_rental_days,
  MIN(r.rental_date) AS first_rental_date,
  MAX(r.rental_date) AS last_rental_date
FROM rental r
GROUP BY r.inventory_id

params.description: Per-inventory aggregated rental metrics: count of rentals, total rental-days, and first/last rental date for each inventory_id.
params.when_to_use: Get the rental history summary for each physical inventory item (inventory_id). | Join inventory-level rental metrics to inventory, film, or store dimensions when you need one row per inventory_id. | Filter inventories by activity (e.g., inventory items with rental_count > 0 or last_rental_date in last N days).
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to a table that is many-to-one FROM inventory (e.g., joining inventory -> rental details) expecting per-rental rows — doing so will undercount/overcount because this view is already aggregated to inventory_id (grain mismatch). | Using this view to answer customer-level or film-level questions without first rolling up or re-aggregating — e.g., summing rental_count across inventories to get film-level counts is valid only if you aggregate after joining to film; joining to a film view that duplicates inventory rows (one-to-many) without re-aggregation will multiply counts. | Treating total_rental_days as a precise duration for partially returned rentals: the SQL computes days only when both rental_date and return_date are NOT NULL, otherwise contributes 0. Relying on it to measure in-progress rental durations is incorrect. | Assuming rental_count equals number of distinct customers or payments — rental_count is count(rental_id) and does not deduplicate by customer_id or payment_id.
params.output_schema: inventory_id: inventory.inventory_id — the unique identifier for the physical inventory item (the aggregation key / grain). | rental_count: COUNT(r.rental_id) — number of rental records associated with this inventory_id (integer). | total_rental_days: SUM(CASE WHEN r.return_date IS NOT NULL AND r.rental_date IS NOT NULL THEN (julianday(r.return_date) - julianday(r.rental_date)) ELSE 0 END) — sum of rental durations in days for rentals with both rental_date and return_date present; rentals missing dates contribute 0. | first_rental_date: MIN(r.rental_date) — earliest rental_date for this inventory_id (null if no rentals). | last_rental_date: MAX(r.rental_date) — most recent rental_date for this inventory_id (null if no rentals).
params.metric: rental_count = COUNT(rental.rental_id) | total_rental_days = SUM(CASE WHEN rental.return_date IS NOT NULL AND rental.rental_date IS NOT NULL THEN (julianday(rental.return_date) - julianday(rental.rental_date)) ELSE 0 END) | first_rental_date = MIN(rental.rental_date) | last_rental_date = MAX(rental.rental_date)
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to inventory_with_film_store (or the base inventory table) on inventory_id — inventory_with_film_store is one-row-per-inventory_id, so joining preserves this view's measures without duplication. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to film_with_language_category via inventory_with_film_store -> film_id (but only after joining inventory_with_film_store). If you perform a direct join that would expand inventory_id to multiple film rows (unlikely), ensure the join is one-to-one. | Do NOT join directly to a payments or rental-detail-level table (one-to-many to this view) without re-aggregating: joining to payments_by_customer_agg is okay only when joining on customer-level keys after appropriate aggregation — joining this view to a table that has multiple rows per inventory_id will multiply rental_count and total_rental_days. | Do NOT join to top_actors_by_film_count_rank or other film-actor ranking outputs on film_id without confirming those sibling views are at film-level (one-to-many relationships from film to actors will cause duplication of inventory-level metrics). If you need actor-level breakdowns, first re-aggregate rentals to film_id, then join to actor-level outputs. | When combining with customer-level views (e.g., customer_with_location or payments_by_customer_agg), join on customer_id only after you have a customer-level aggregation; joining this inventory-aggregated view to customer rows directly will be meaningless because inventory_id <> customer_id keys differ. | If you need store-level aggregates: aggregate this view (e.g., SUM(rental_count) GROUP BY store_id after joining inventory -> store) rather than joining store -> inventory and expecting this view's rows to expand correctly.
params.comparison: Use latest_rental_per_inventory_rank instead when you need the single most recent rental row per inventory (rental_id and full rental record) rather than aggregated counts and sums — latest_rental_per_inventory_rank is record-level and preserves per-rental attributes. | Use payments_by_customer_agg when your question is about customer payment metrics (amounts, counts) rather than inventory rental activity; payments_by_customer_agg is aggregated by customer_id, not inventory_id. | Use inventory_with_film_store when you need inventory attributes (film_id, store_id, etc.) alongside these rental metrics; join inventory_with_film_store to this view on inventory_id to combine attributes safely. | Use film_with_language_category when your analysis needs film-level metadata (title, language, category). If the objective is film-level rental metrics, aggregate this view up to film_id after joining through inventory_with_film_store instead of using rentals_by_inventory_agg directly.

views.description: Aggregated rental activity per inventory item: rental_count, total_rental_duration (in days, where return_date - rental_date), first and last rental dates. One row per inventory_id. Useful to measure item utilization and turnover. | Use for: Which inventory items are rented most often; Compute average rental duration per inventory or film; Identify unused inventory (rental_count = 0) by LEFT JOINing inventory

views.name: top_actors_by_film_count_rank
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  a.actor_id,
  a.first_name,
  a.last_name,
  COUNT(DISTINCT fa.film_id) AS actor_film_count,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT fa.film_id) DESC) AS actor_rank
FROM actor a
LEFT JOIN film_actor fa ON a.actor_id = fa.actor_id
GROUP BY a.actor_id, a.first_name, a.last_name

params.description: Ranks actors (actor_id) by the number of distinct films they appear in, returning each actor's film count and rank.
params.when_to_use: Find the top actors by distinct film appearances (e.g., leaderboards of actors with most films). | Report each actor's film count and their rank relative to other actors by that count. | Drive UI lists that show actor name, number of films, and position (rank) among actors.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to a table that is one-to-many to actor (e.g., film_actor, rentals) without re-aggregation — doing so will duplicate rows and inflate counts because this view is already aggregated at actor_id. | Using it to answer questions about film-level or role-level details (e.g., which films or which roles) — the view's grain is actor_id, not film_id or role. | Using it to compute time-cohorted counts (e.g., films per actor in a year) — the view's counts are global across all films and not partitioned by time or cohort. | Assuming actor_film_count is a simple row count of film_actor rows — it is COUNT(DISTINCT fa.film_id), so if film_actor contains duplicate film_id rows for the same actor (data quality issues), the distinct prevents overcount; removing DISTINCT will change meaning.
params.output_schema: actor_id: Unique identifier for the actor. Source: actor.actor_id (base table). | first_name: Actor's first name. Source: actor.first_name (base table). | last_name: Actor's last name. Source: actor.last_name (base table). | actor_film_count: Number of distinct films the actor appears in. Source/definition: COUNT(DISTINCT film_actor.film_id) aggregated per actor_id. | actor_rank: Rank of the actor ordered by actor_film_count descending. Source/definition: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT film_actor.film_id) DESC) computed at the actor-level.
params.metric: actor_film_count = COUNT(DISTINCT film_actor.film_id)  -- aggregate per actor_id | actor_rank = RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(DISTINCT film_actor.film_id) DESC)  -- windowed rank computed after aggregation by actor
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to actor-level one-row-per-actor dimensions or lookups (e.g., an actor_profile view keyed by actor_id that is guaranteed one row per actor) on actor_id — safe because this view is one row per actor_id and joining a 1:1 dimension will not duplicate measures. | Do NOT join directly to film_actor or any other one-to-many table on actor_id (e.g., film_actor, rentals, inventory) without re-aggregating the joined data first — those joins will duplicate the aggregated actor_film_count and produce incorrect inflated measures. | If you must combine with film-level details, join this view to an aggregated film-side view keyed to actor_id (for example, a per-actor film-genre breakdown that is aggregated to actor_id) so both sides are at the same grain and measures remain accurate. | When joining to sibling JOIN-type views (e.g., film_with_language_category, staff_activity_join), ensure those sibling views are either 1:1 per actor_id or are pre-aggregated to actor_id; otherwise re-aggregate after the join. | If you need to compute conditional counts (e.g., films in a given year), compute a separate aggregated metric (COUNT(DISTINCT film_id) FILTER (WHERE ...) grouped by actor_id) rather than filtering after this view and re-counting without adjusting for duplication.
params.comparison: use film_with_language_category instead when you need film-level attributes (language, category) joined to films — that sibling is a JOIN across film-related tables and is film-grained, while this view is actor-grained. | use inventory_with_film_store when your analysis is inventory/store oriented (store or inventory-level metrics) — that view is inventory/film-store oriented and not actor-grained. | use customer_with_location, payments_by_customer_agg, rentals_by_inventory_agg, customer_payment_rfm when you need customer- or rental-centric aggregations or windows — those siblings are customer- or rental-grained and contain time/monetary metrics this view does not. | use latest_rental_per_inventory_rank when you need per-inventory ranking of rentals over time — that sibling is a RANK view at inventory/rental grain and is not appropriate for actor film counts. | use film_length_and_rate_norm when you need normalized film length/rate metrics — that is a film-level normalized metric set, not actor-level counts.

views.description: Actor-level ranking by number of distinct films an actor appears in. One row per actor with actor_film_count and actor_rank (dense). Useful for top-K actor queries and actor-based filtering. | Use for: Top-N actors by number of films; Filter actors by rank or count for reports

views.name: customer_payment_rfm
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.customer_id,
  p.payment_count,
  p.total_payment_amount,
  p.first_payment_date,
  p.last_payment_date,
  CASE WHEN p.last_payment_date IS NOT NULL THEN (julianday('now') - julianday(p.last_payment_date)) ELSE NULL END AS recency_days,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY p.total_payment_amount DESC) AS monetary_rank,
  SUM(p.total_payment_amount) OVER (ORDER BY p.total_payment_amount DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cumulative_revenue_ordered_by_monetary
FROM (
  SELECT
    p.customer_id,
    COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payment_count,
    SUM(p.amount) AS total_payment_amount,
    MIN(p.payment_date) AS first_payment_date,
    MAX(p.payment_date) AS last_payment_date
  FROM payment p
  GROUP BY p.customer_id
) p

params.description: Per-customer RFM-style summary: counts, amounts, first/last payment dates, recency in days, monetary rank, and running cumulative revenue ordered by monetary.
params.when_to_use: Identify customers by total payments and recency for segmentation or RFM analysis (one row per customer). | Rank customers by monetary contribution and compute cumulative revenue shares ordered by monetary. | Join customer-level attributes to payments-based customer metrics (e.g., enrich with customer demographics) without changing metric semantics.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to transaction-level tables (e.g., payment) to compute additional counts/amounts per payment row — this will double-count or change aggregates because this view is already aggregated to customer_id. | Using it to analyze time-windowed cohorts (e.g., payments in last 30 days) — the view aggregates across all payments in the underlying payment table and contains no built-in date filter; applying a post-join date filter will not re-aggregate correctly for cohort counts. | Joining to one-to-many child tables (e.g., multiple addresses per customer) without first reducing them to one row per customer — such joins will multiply rows and thus silently inflate measures like payment_count and total_payment_amount. | Treating monetary_rank or cumulative_revenue_ordered_by_monetary as stable across different partitions — these window calculations are computed across the entire result set as written and will change if the result set is filtered or partitioned differently.
params.output_schema: customer_id: unique customer identifier; derives from payment.customer_id (base column). This is the grain of the view (one row per customer_id). | payment_count: number of payments made by the customer; derives from COUNT(payment.payment_id) in the inner aggregation. | total_payment_amount: sum of payment amounts for the customer; derives from SUM(payment.amount) in the inner aggregation. | first_payment_date: earliest payment_date for the customer; derives from MIN(payment.payment_date) in the inner aggregation. | last_payment_date: latest payment_date for the customer; derives from MAX(payment.payment_date) in the inner aggregation. | recency_days: days since last_payment_date to 'now' (CURRENT DATE) computed as julianday('now') - julianday(last_payment_date); NULL when last_payment_date is NULL. | monetary_rank: rank of the customer by total_payment_amount in descending order (ties receive same rank) computed with RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_payment_amount DESC). | cumulative_revenue_ordered_by_monetary: running cumulative sum of total_payment_amount ordered by total_payment_amount DESC computed with SUM(total_payment_amount) OVER (ORDER BY total_payment_amount DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
params.metric: payment_count = COUNT(payment.payment_id)  -- number of payment rows per customer (inner GROUP BY payment.customer_id). | total_payment_amount = SUM(payment.amount)  -- total monetary value per customer (inner GROUP BY payment.customer_id). | first_payment_date = MIN(payment.payment_date)  -- earliest payment_date per customer. | last_payment_date = MAX(payment.payment_date)  -- latest payment_date per customer. | recency_days = CASE WHEN last_payment_date IS NOT NULL THEN (julianday('now') - julianday(last_payment_date)) ELSE NULL END  -- derived measure in outer select, expressed in days relative to query execution time. | monetary_rank = RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_payment_amount DESC)  -- rank across the resultset by total_payment_amount, ties get same rank. | cumulative_revenue_ordered_by_monetary = SUM(total_payment_amount) OVER (ORDER BY total_payment_amount DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)  -- running total ordered by descending monetary value.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customer_with_location on customer_id — safe because this view is one-row-per-customer_id, and customer_with_location should be one-row-per-customer_id (enriching attributes does not duplicate measures). | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to staff_activity_join on staff_id only after aggregating staff side to one row per staff_id if you plan to roll up by staff; do NOT join directly if staff_activity_join is one-to-many relative to customer_id. | do NOT join to payment (the raw payment table) on customer_id without re-aggregating the payment side first — joining would reconnect aggregated customer rows to multiple payment rows and multiply payment_count and total_payment_amount. | do NOT join to rentals_by_inventory_agg or any other one-to-many view by customer_id (if that sibling aggregates by inventory or rental id) without re-aggregation to customer_id first — multiplicative duplication of metrics will occur. | If you need to combine with a table that is one-to-many to customer (for example, multiple addresses or orders), pre-aggregate that table to one row per customer_id (e.g., COUNT or MAX) and then join; alternatively, join first and then re-aggregate at customer-level but be explicit about aggregation to avoid silent mis-counts.
params.comparison: use payments_by_customer_agg instead when you need only base aggregations at customer level without the additional RANK and cumulative window measures — payments_by_customer_agg (AGG) likely provides the raw aggregates (payment_count, total_payment_amount, first/last dates) and is preferable if you want stable aggregates independent of window ranking. | use customer_with_location when you need location/demographic attributes alongside customer metrics — join this view to customer_with_location for enrichment but prefer customer_with_location as the primary source when queries are keyed by geography. | do not use this view when you need inventory- or rental-level analyses — use rentals_by_inventory_agg or inventory_with_film_store siblings which are aggregated/joined at inventory/film/store grain appropriate for those questions. | use top_actors_by_film_count_rank or latest_rental_per_inventory_rank for rank-style analyses within their specific grains (actors or inventory); those siblings compute rank within their domain, while this view ranks customers by monetary contribution.

views.description: RFM-style measures with recency (days since last payment), frequency and monetary and running_total over customers ordered by total_payment_amount. One row per customer. Useful for segmentation and cumulative revenue analysis. | Use for: RFM segmentation and recency/frequency/monetary calculations; Cumulative revenue contribution by customers

views.name: latest_rental_per_inventory_rank
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  r.rental_id,
  r.inventory_id,
  r.customer_id,
  r.rental_date,
  r.return_date,
  r.staff_id,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY r.inventory_id ORDER BY r.rental_date DESC) AS inventory_rental_rank
FROM rental r

params.description: For each rental event on an inventory item, returns the rental row and a rank of that rental per inventory ordered by most recent rental_date (1 = latest).
params.when_to_use: Find the most recent rental(s) per inventory item (e.g., inventory_rental_rank = 1) | Filter or join on the latest N rentals per inventory item (top-N per inventory) | Analyze rental history at the rental-event grain while needing a per-inventory recency rank
params.when_not_to_use: Use this view to compute aggregates per inventory (e.g., total rentals per inventory) — WHY: this view is at the rental-event grain and contains one row per rental; aggregating without explicit GROUP BY risks misinterpreting the rank as a pre-aggregated measure. | Use this view as if it were one-row-per-inventory (inventory grain) — WHY: grain is ['inventory_id', 'rental_id']; selecting inventory_id alone will produce multiple rows per inventory and operations expecting single inventory rows (e.g., joins that assume uniqueness) will produce duplication. | Join this view to other one-to-many children (e.g., payments) without re-aggregation — WHY: joining to tables that have multiple rows per rental_id or inventory_id will multiply rows and counts unless you aggregate first or join on a unique key. | Use the rank column as a stable identifier of 'latest' without filtering — WHY: rank is computed in-window and must be filtered (e.g., =1) to get the latest; leaving rank unfiltered while aggregating will not collapse to latest rental automatically.
params.output_schema: rental_id: primary key of the rental event from rental.rental_id | inventory_id: identifier of the inventory item from rental.inventory_id | customer_id: identifier of the customer who made the rental from rental.customer_id | rental_date: timestamp/datetime when the rental started from rental.rental_date | return_date: timestamp/datetime when the rental was returned from rental.return_date | staff_id: staff who processed the rental from rental.staff_id | inventory_rental_rank: integer rank per inventory computed as RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rental.inventory_id ORDER BY rental.rental_date DESC) — 1 is the most recent rental for that inventory
params.grounded_columns: rental.rental_id | rental.inventory_id | rental.customer_id | rental.rental_date | rental.return_date | rental.staff_id
params.metric: inventory_rental_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rental.inventory_id ORDER BY rental.rental_date DESC)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to inventory_with_film_store on inventory_id — safe because inventory_with_film_store is expected to be one-row-per-inventory, so joining does NOT duplicate rental rows (the view remains at rental-event grain). | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to film_with_language_category on inventory_with_film_store.film_id (via inventory join) — safe only if you traverse inventory -> film (one-to-one per inventory to film) and do not cause additional multiplicity. | do NOT join directly to rentals_by_inventory_agg (AGG) expecting additional detail — rentals_by_inventory_agg is aggregated per inventory; if you join it to this view (rental-event grain) you will replicate aggregated values across each rental row unless you join carefully and expect repeated aggregate values per rental. | do NOT join this view to payments_by_customer_agg or customer_payment_rfm without care — these sibling aggregates are at the customer level; joining on customer_id will repeat those customer-aggregates for every rental of that customer (safe only if repeating aggregate values per rental is intended). | do NOT join to one-to-many children of rental (e.g., a hypothetical rental_items or payment rows) without pre-aggregating those children back to rental_id — otherwise the number of rows (and any counts/sums) will be multiplied.
params.comparison: use rentals_by_inventory_agg instead when you need aggregated metrics per inventory (e.g., total_rentals, last_rental_date) — it returns one row per inventory and avoids dealing with rental-level duplicates. | use staff_activity_join when your goal is staff-level activity summaries — staff_activity_join is tailored for staff aggregations, whereas this view is at the rental-event grain and only contains the staff_id per rental. | use customer_with_location when you need customer demographic/location attributes — join this view to that view for location-enriched rental events; if you only need customer-level info without per-rental detail, prefer customer_with_location alone. | use top_actors_by_film_count_rank or film_length_and_rate_norm when analyzing film-level ranks/normalizations — those siblings operate at film-level grains and are not appropriate for per-rental recency ranking.

views.description: For each inventory_id, the most recent rental (by rental_date). One row per inventory rental instance with per-inventory rank; downstream filters can select the latest (rank = 1). Useful for identifying current renter or most recent activity per item. | Use for: Find most recent rental per inventory item; Identify currently rented items (latest rental with NULL return_date)

views.name: staff_activity_join
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.staff_id,
  s.first_name,
  s.last_name,
  s.address_id,
  a.address AS address,
  a.city_id AS city_id,
  ci.city AS city,
  ci.country_id AS country_id,
  co.country AS country,
  s.email,
  s.store_id,
  s.active,
  s.username,
  s.last_update
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
LEFT JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
LEFT JOIN country co ON ci.country_id = co.country_id

params.description: A denormalized, one-row-per-staff lookup of staff person attributes and their linked address/city/country text values.
params.when_to_use: Look up staff attributes (name, contact, store, active flag, username) along with human-readable address, city and country for display or filtering. | Join to transactional data at the staff_id grain when you need staff descriptive attributes to label measures that are already at staff_id (for example, staff-level aggregates of payments or counts). | Export or feed a UI/select list of staff with their location context (address, city, country) without needing additional joins.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to a table that is many-to-one from staff (for example, payments, rentals or inventories) if you expect aggregated staff-level measures to remain correct — doing so without aggregation will multiply rows and over-count (grain mismatch). | Using this view to answer cohort or time-series questions (e.g., "active staff this month") because it contains no temporal versioning of staff attributes (last_update is an attribute timestamp but does not represent a history of status over time). | Attempting to compute aggregated metrics here (e.g., total_payments) — this view is not an aggregate and contains no sum/count columns; adding aggregates here without changing grain will cause silent mis-counts. | Treating address/city/country as independent dimensions (e.g., joining independently to address and country by different keys) — the view already resolves them via the chain staff.address_id -> address.city_id -> city.country_id; rejoining differently can produce inconsistent or duplicated rows.
params.output_schema: staff_id: staff.staff_id — primary key of this view; identifies one staff row. | first_name: staff.first_name — staff given name from staff table. | last_name: staff.last_name — staff family name from staff table. | address_id: staff.address_id — foreign key on staff referencing address.address_id (nullable if staff has no address). | address: address.address — textual street/address from address table (aliased as address). | city_id: address.city_id — foreign key on address referencing city.city_id (nullable if address has no city). | city: city.city — city name from city table. | country_id: city.country_id — foreign key on city referencing country.country_id (nullable if city has no country). | country: country.country — country name from country table. | email: staff.email — staff contact email from staff table. | store_id: staff.store_id — fk to store indicating which store the staff belongs to. | active: staff.active — boolean/tinyint active flag from staff table. | username: staff.username — staff system username from staff table. | last_update: staff.last_update — timestamp of last update for staff row (from staff table).
params.grounded_columns: staff.staff_id | staff.first_name | staff.last_name | staff.address_id | address.address_id | address.address | address.city_id | city.city_id | city.city | city.country_id | country.country_id | country.country | staff.email | staff.store_id | staff.active | staff.username | staff.last_update
params.metric: This view exposes no derived numeric aggregates. All columns are base attributes directly selected from the underlying tables. | If you need a derived metric at staff grain, compute it from a properly aggregated source and then join to this view on staff_id. Example pattern (outside this view): staff_total_payments = SUM(payments.amount) GROUP BY payments.staff_id
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension/lookups keyed by staff_id — e.g., join staff_activity_join to a staff-level aggregate view (payments_by_staff_agg) ON staff_activity_join.staff_id = payments_by_staff_agg.staff_id — safe because payments_by_staff_agg is already aggregated to one row per staff, so measures will not be duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE: join to store lookup on staff_activity_join.store_id = store.store_id — safe because store is one row per store and this view is one row per staff. | do NOT join this view directly to raw many-to-one child tables (payments, rental, inventory) without first aggregating the child table to staff_id. For example, joining staff_activity_join to payments (payments.staff_id) will duplicate the staff row once per payment and over-count any staff-level measures unless payments are aggregated to staff-level first. | do NOT join to other one-to-many results (e.g., customer lists, film lists) without aggregation because staff_activity_join's grain is staff_id; joining to anything with multiple rows per staff will multiply this view's row count and produce incorrect counts/sums. | If you must bring back child-level rows, use explicit aggregations or windowed deduplication (e.g., latest_rental_per_inventory_rank) and then join on staff_id after ensuring the child side is reduced to one row per staff or one row per desired key.
params.comparison: use customer_with_location when you need customer attributes and location context rather than staff — that view is analogous but at customer granularity. | use film_with_language_category or inventory_with_film_store when you need film or inventory contextual attributes; those siblings are at different grains (film, inventory) and contain film-specific joins/columns. | use payments_by_customer_agg or rentals_by_inventory_agg when you need pre-aggregated monetary or count metrics — those sibling AGG views already prevent duplication when joined to lookup dimensions like this staff view. | use latest_rental_per_inventory_rank or top_actors_by_film_count_rank when you require ranked/deduplicated rows from many-to-many relationships — these RANK views handle de-duplication patterns that this simple join view does not. | This view differs from its siblings by being a pure join-based lookup at the staff_id grain with no aggregates, ranks or normalization. It should be treated as a descriptive dimension for staff only, not as a source of metrics.

views.description: Staff members with their store and address/city/country context. One row per staff. Useful for staff performance joins to rentals/payments and regional staffing reports. | Use for: Staff lists by region or store; Join staff to rentals/payments for performance metrics

views.name: film_length_and_rate_norm
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  f.film_id,
  f.title,
  f.description,
  CASE WHEN f.release_year = '' THEN NULL ELSE f.release_year END AS release_year,
  f.language_id,
  f.rental_duration,
  CAST(f.rental_rate AS NUMERIC) AS rental_rate,
  CAST(f.length AS NUMERIC) AS length,
  CAST(f.replacement_cost AS NUMERIC) AS replacement_cost,
  CASE WHEN CAST(f.length AS NUMERIC) > 0 THEN (CAST(f.replacement_cost AS NUMERIC) / CAST(f.length AS NUMERIC)) ELSE NULL END AS cost_per_minute,
  f.rating,
  f.special_features,
  f.last_update
FROM film f

params.description: Per-film normalized attributes and a simple per-minute replacement-cost metric for each film (one row per film_id).
params.when_to_use: Retrieving film-level attributes (title, description, release_year, language_id, rental_duration, rental_rate, length, replacement_cost, rating, special_features, last_update) for reporting or lookups keyed by film_id. | Computing per-film cost efficiency (replacement_cost per minute) for individual films or for sets of films after applying filters and then aggregating outside this view. | Joining film-level attributes to dimension tables where the join key is film_id (one-to-one) or to other one-row-per-film objects.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view as a pre-aggregated source for customer-, inventory-, store-, or payment-level metrics (e.g., total revenue, rental counts) — those are different grains and would cause mis-counts if you aggregate here without accounting for multiplicity. | Do not join this view directly to one-to-many tables (for example inventory, rentals, payments) expecting measures here to remain unique per film. Joining to many-rows-per-film sources will duplicate film rows and silently inflate any downstream sums/averages unless you re-aggregate or deduplicate first. | Do not use cost_per_minute as if it were an aggregate across a cohort of films without re-weighting; cost_per_minute is a per-film ratio (replacement_cost / length) and averaging that ratio across films is different from computing total_replacement_cost / total_length. | Avoid treating release_year blank string ('') as a valid year — the view coerces empty string to NULL. Consumers expecting numeric years must handle NULLs.
params.output_schema: film_id: primary key of the view and film identifier, source: film.film_id | title: film title string, source: film.title | description: film description text, source: film.description | release_year: release year as stored in film.release_year, but empty-string normalized to NULL (CASE WHEN '' THEN NULL), source: film.release_year | language_id: foreign key to language, source: film.language_id | rental_duration: rental duration (days or units as modeled), source: film.rental_duration | rental_rate: rental rate cast to NUMERIC, source: CAST(film.rental_rate AS NUMERIC) | length: film length cast to NUMERIC, source: CAST(film.length AS NUMERIC) | replacement_cost: replacement cost cast to NUMERIC, source: CAST(film.replacement_cost AS NUMERIC) | cost_per_minute: per-film derived metric replacement_cost / length, NULL when length <= 0, source: CASE WHEN length > 0 THEN replacement_cost/length ELSE NULL END (using the CAST numeric columns) | rating: MPAA rating or equivalent, source: film.rating | special_features: film special_features (likely a string or array), source: film.special_features | last_update: last update timestamp for the film record, source: film.last_update
params.grounded_columns: film.film_id | film.title | film.description | film.release_year | film.language_id | film.rental_duration | film.rental_rate | film.length | film.replacement_cost | film.rating | film.special_features | film.last_update
params.metric: rental_rate = CAST(film.rental_rate AS NUMERIC) | length = CAST(film.length AS NUMERIC) | replacement_cost = CAST(film.replacement_cost AS NUMERIC) | cost_per_minute = CASE WHEN CAST(film.length AS NUMERIC) > 0 THEN (CAST(film.replacement_cost AS NUMERIC) / CAST(film.length AS NUMERIC)) ELSE NULL END
params.composition: Safe to join: language dimension (e.g., language table or a one-row-per-language view) on language_id — joining will not duplicate film rows because film.language_id is a single scalar per film. | Safe to join: any one-to-one film-level enrichment view keyed by film_id (for example, a supplemental film_metadata view where film_id is unique) — safe because the cardinality remains one-row-per-film. | Do NOT join without care to inventory, rentals, payments, or other one-to-many tables on film_id (examples: inventory_with_film_store, rentals_by_inventory_agg if not pre-aggregated to film) because those contain multiple rows per film and will multiply film rows and any downstream aggregates; instead either: | - join to an aggregated version of the many-side that is explicitly grouped to film_id (e.g., rentals aggregated per film_id), or | - join using EXISTS/subquery or use DISTINCT/ROW_NUMBER to avoid multiplicative duplication before aggregating. | When composing measures: cost_per_minute is a per-row (film-level) ratio. To compute a correct overall cost per minute across multiple films, compute total_replacement_cost / total_length after joining/filtering, not AVG(cost_per_minute), unless an unweighted mean is intended.
params.comparison: use film_with_language_category (JOIN) instead when you need the film record enriched with language name and category(s) in a single flattened row — that sibling already joins language/category and is convenient when you need those descriptive dims together. | use inventory_with_film_store (JOIN) when you need stock/inventory and store-level information alongside film attributes; note that inventory_with_film_store will increase row-count per film (one row per inventory unit) so it's suitable when you intend to analyze per-inventory-unit measures. | use rentals_by_inventory_agg or payments_by_customer_agg (AGG) when you need aggregated rental/payment metrics; those siblings are already at aggregated grains (rentals/payments) and avoid manual aggregation mistakes that would occur if you joined this film-level view to raw rental/payment rows. | use top_actors_by_film_count_rank / latest_rental_per_inventory_rank / customer_payment_rfm (RANK/WIN) when you need ranking/window analytics; those siblings compute window functions and are not substitutes for simple film attribute lookup. | In short: choose this view for canonical, normalized per-film attributes and per-film cost_per_minute; choose sibling JOIN/AGG/RANK views when you need their specific enriched, aggregated, or windowed shapes to avoid re-implementing joins/aggregations and risk of duplication.

views.description: Normalized film attributes with canonical numeric casts and a derived length_minutes and cost_per_minute. One row per film. Useful for numeric comparisons and filters on film length and rates. | Use for: Compare films by length or rental_rate; Filter films by cost_per_minute or length thresholds; Compute aggregates like average length or average rental_rate
